title: Al-Wakil, the Trustee
hook: the Trustee, the one you hand things over to, after doing your part (Tirmidhi)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash-Shakur, the Appreciative. Your line was nothing small is lost. Did you thank someone out loud for something tiny? Day two hundred fifty-three.

A man comes to see the Prophet. He gets off his camel, and stops. He's got a question, and it's a real one. Should he tie the camel up, and then trust God to keep it? Or should he leave it loose, and trust God, full stop? If he ties it, is he trusting less? If he doesn't, is he being a fool? You've had your own version of this. You studied, or you didn't. You locked the door, or you didn't. How much is on you, and how much do you hand over? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave him an answer in four words that people still quote more than fourteen centuries later. Today: tawakkul.
screen: `A MAN AND HIS CAMEL.` → `TIE IT, OR TRUST?` → `FOUR WORDS.`

segments.voice: The answer, in the collection of at-Tirmidhi: tie it, and trust. Both. In that order. Tawakkul is the word for that trust, and it comes from the same root as today's name, al-Wakil, the Trustee. In ordinary Arabic, a wakil is the person you hand your affairs to: an agent, a representative, the one who handles it when you can't. Calling God al-Wakil means he is the One you hand things over to. But the hadith sets the order. First you do your part. Tie the rope. Study for the test. See the doctor. Then you let go of the outcome, because it was never fully in your hands. That's tawakkul. Not doing nothing. Doing what's yours, and then letting the rest rest. The Qur'an promises, in Pickthall's words: "And whosoever putteth his trust in Allah, He will suffice him." Another hadith in Tirmidhi adds a picture. If you trusted God as you truly should, he would provide for you as he provides for the birds: they go out hungry in the morning and come back full at evening. Notice, the birds go out. They don't sit in the nest waiting. And there's a phrase many Muslims say when things are heavy: hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil. God is enough for us, and he is the best Trustee. The Qur'an gives it to believers who were told an army was gathering against them. It's said after the work is done, when there's nothing left to do but hand it over.
screen: `TIE IT, AND TRUST.` · `A WAKIL HANDLES YOUR AFFAIRS.` · `THE BIRDS GO OUT.` · `GOD IS ENOUGH FOR US.` · then, large: `TIE THE CAMEL, THEN TRUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do your part, then hand it over. Sit, and think of one thing you're worried about. Ask yourself honestly: what's the rope I can tie? One email, one call, one appointment, one conversation. Name it, and decide when you'll do it. Then look at what's left, the part that isn't yours to control. Picture setting it down. If you pray, you can say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil. If not, just breathe out, and let it rest. The bell holds the time.
Tawakkul. Trust in God, from the same root as al-Wakil, the Trustee: do your part, then hand over the rest. Today's word.
Your line: tie the camel, then trust. Today, tie your one rope, and then, when the worry comes back, remind it that the rest is handed over. Day two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims describe tawakkul as taking every reasonable step and then relying on God for the outcome, and many say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil in hard moments.

fork.setup: you have come to see the Prophet. your camel is standing there. you want to trust God completely. what do you do with the camel?
options: leave it loose. trust means not tying it.
fork.reveal: tie it, and trust: the Prophet's answer in at-Tirmidhi. doing your part is part of the trust.

original.note: Arabic: trust, reliance on God. the same root as al-Wakil, the Trustee.

trapdoor: what you thought: let go and let God.
what it means: tie the camel, then trust. do your part, then hand the outcome to the Trustee.
what a scholar hears: w-k-l: a wakil is an agent you delegate to. the tie-it-and-trust hadith is in at-Tirmidhi, and scholars use it against passive fatalism.
